claim: NGLY1 is proposed to remove N-glycans from misfolded N-glycoproteins after their retrotranslocation from the ER to the cytosol during ERAD.
source: During endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation (ERAD), the cytoplasmic enzyme N-glycanase 1 (NGLY1) is proposed to remove N-glycans from misfolded N-glycoproteins after their retrotranslocation from the ER to the cytosol.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a proposed mechanism based on existing literature.

claim: NGLY1 regulates Drosophila BMP signaling in a tissue-specific manner.
source: We previously reported that NGLY1 regulates Drosophila BMP signaling in a tissue-specific manner (Galeone et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Drosophila Dpp and mouse BMP4 are biologically relevant targets of NGLY1.
source: Here, we establish the Drosophila Dpp and its mouse ortholog BMP4 as biologically relevant targets of NGLY1
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Accumulation of misfolded BMP4 in the ER results in ER stress.
source: Accumulation of misfolded BMP4 in the ER results in ER stress and prompts the ER recruitment of NGLY1.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data showing increased ER stress markers (GRP78, pIRE1α, OS9) in Figure 4.

claim: Accumulation of misfolded BMP4 in the ER prompts the ER recruitment of NGLY1.
source: Accumulation of misfolded BMP4 in the ER results in ER stress and prompts the ER recruitment of NGLY1.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5 showing NGLY1 colocalization with ER marker upon BMP4 transfection.

claim: ER-associated NGLY1 deglycosylates misfolded BMP4 molecules to promote their retrotranslocation and proteasomal degradation.
source: The ER-associated NGLY1 then deglycosylates misfolded BMP4 molecules to promote their retrotranslocation and proteasomal degradation, thereby allowing properly-folded BMP4 molecules to proceed through the secretory pathway and activate signaling in other cells.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that VCP-binding mutants of NGLY1 fail to rescue BMP4 signaling (Figure 6) and that proteasome inhibition leads to accumulation of deglycosylated BMP4 (Figure 6D).

claim: Deglycosylation of misfolded BMP4 by NGLY1 allows properly-folded BMP4 molecules to proceed through the secretory pathway and activate signaling in other cells.
source: The ER-associated NGLY1 then deglycosylates misfolded BMP4 molecules to promote their retrotranslocation and proteasomal degradation, thereby allowing properly-folded BMP4 molecules to proceed through the secretory pathway and activate signaling in other cells.
evidence: This is supported by data showing impaired BMP4 secretion and signaling in Ngly1-/- MEFs (Figures 3 and 4).

claim: Impaired BMP4 signaling might underlie some of the NGLY1 deficiency patient phenotypes.
source: Our study redefines the role of NGLY1 during ERAD and suggests that impaired BMP4 signaling might underlie some of the NGLY1 deficiency patient phenotypes.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the findings in the manuscript and known patient phenotypes.

claim: NGLY1 is a cytoplasmic enzyme capable of removing N-glycans from glycoproteins.
source: N-Glycanase 1 (NGLY1; also known as peptide:N-glycanase or PNGase) is a cytoplasmic enzyme capable of removing N-glycans from glycoproteins (Suzuki et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Mutations in human NGLY1 cause an autosomal recessive, multi-system developmental disorder called NGLY1 deficiency.
source: Mutations in human NGLY1 cause an autosomal recessive, multi-system developmental disorder called NGLY1 deficiency (OMIM # 610661) (Need et al., 2012; Enns et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: NGLY1 and its homologs recognize and cleave N-glycans from their target proteins, changing the asparagine (N) to aspartic acid (D) upon removing the sugar chain.
source: NGLY1 and its homologs recognize and cleave N-glycans from their target proteins, changing the asparagine (N) to aspartic acid (D) upon removing the sugar chain (Hirayama et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: N-Glycans are added to proteins in the ER and undergo trimming and maturation in the ER and in the Golgi apparatus.
source: N-Glycans are added to proteins in the ER and undergo trimming and maturation in the ER and in the Golgi apparatus, where the properly folded proteins are sorted toward various cellular destinations (Taniguchi and Aebi, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Proteins that fail to fold properly are recognized, retrotranslocated from the ER into the cytosol and undergo proteasomal degradation through ERAD.
source: However, proteins that fail to fold properly are recognized, retrotranslocated from the ER into the cytosol and undergo proteasomal degradation through a process called ER-associated degradation (ERAD) (Smith et al., 2011; Brodsky, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The yeast NGLY1 homolog (PNG1) is part of the ERAD mechanism.
source: The yeast NGLY1 homolog (PNG1) is part of the ERAD mechanism (Hirayama et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: NGLY1 is proposed to contribute to ERAD by removing N-glycans from misfolded proteins after their retrotranslocation, thereby promoting their degradation.
source: NGLY1 is proposed to contribute to ERAD by removing N-glycans from misfolded proteins after their retrotranslocation, thereby promoting their degradation (Suzuki et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism from the literature that the manuscript challenges.

claim: A fraction of NGLY1 molecules are associated with the ER.
source: A fraction of NGLY1 molecules are associated with the ER (Suzuki et al., 1997a; Katiyar et al., 2004), likely through protein-protein interaction with valosin containing protein (VCP; also called p97) (Ye et al., 2001; Li et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: NGLY1 is likely associated with the ER through protein-protein interaction with VCP.
source: A fraction of NGLY1 molecules are associated with the ER (Suzuki et al., 1997a; Katiyar et al., 2004), likely through protein-protein interaction with valosin containing protein (VCP; also called p97) (Ye et al., 2001; Li et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature and the word 'likely' indicates inference.

claim: The functional significance of NGLY1's ER recruitment is not known.
source: However, the functional significance of NGLY1's ER recruitment is not known, and the temporal relationship between retrotranslocation and deglycosylation has not been determined.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the manuscript addresses.

claim: The temporal relationship between retrotranslocation and deglycosylation has not been determined.
source: However, the functional significance of NGLY1's ER recruitment is not known, and the temporal relationship between retrotranslocation and deglycosylation has not been determined.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the manuscript addresses.

claim: Dpp signaling is responsible for the specification of two regions in the middle part of the Drosophila embryonic intestine: the gastric caeca region and the acid zone.
source: During Drosophila embryonic development, signaling by a bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) called Decapentaplegic (Dpp) is responsible for the specification of two regions in the middle part of the intestine (midgut), the gastric caeca region and the acid zone (Panganiban et al., 1990; Newfeld et al., 1996; Dubreuil, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Dpp is first expressed in narrow bands in parasegments 3 (PS3) and PS7 of the embryonic visceral mesoderm.
source: Dpp is first expressed in narrow bands in parasegments 3 (PS3) and PS7 of the embryonic visceral mesoderm (VM).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Dpp uses a paracrine/autocrine loop to sustain high levels of its own expression in the VM.
source: Dpp then uses a paracrine/autocrine loop to sustain high levels of its own expression in the VM.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: As Dpp level increases in the PS3 and PS7 regions of the VM, it activates BMP signaling in the neighboring endoderm and induces the formation of gastric caeca and acid zone regions of the midgut.
source: As Dpp level increases in the PS3 and PS7 regions of the VM, it activates BMP signaling in the neighboring endoderm and induces the formation of gastric caeca and acid zone regions of the midgut (Panganiban et al., 1990; Hursh et al., 1993; Bienz, 1997; Galeone et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Drosophila Pngl is required in the VM to promote Dpp autoactivation in this tissue and consequently BMP signaling in the midgut endoderm.
source: We have previously shown that the Drosophila homolog of NGLY1 (PNGase-like or Pngl) is required in the VM to promote Dpp autoactivation in this tissue and consequently BMP signaling in the midgut endoderm (Galeone et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The direct target of Pngl in the BMP pathway is not known.
source: However, the direct target of Pngl in the BMP pathway and the mechanism for the regulation of BMP signaling by Pngl are not known.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the manuscript addresses.

claim: The mechanism for the regulation of BMP signaling by Pngl is not known.
source: However, the direct target of Pngl in the BMP pathway and the mechanism for the regulation of BMP signaling by Pngl are not known.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the manuscript addresses.

claim: BMP ligands have a number of N-glycosylation sites, many of which are experimentally verified.
source: BMP ligands have a number of N-glycosylation sites, many of which are experimentally verified (Gelbart, 1989; Groppe et al., 1998; Tauscher et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Upon Pngl knock-down, one of the Dpp-GFP bands shifted upwards, consistent with the presence of N-glycans that would normally be removed by Pngl.
source: Upon Pngl knock-down, one of the Dpp-GFP bands shifted upwards, consistent with the presence of N-glycans that would normally be removed by Pngl.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Incubation of the protein extract from Pngl knock-down animals with PNGase F restored Dpp-GFP migration.
source: Incubation of the protein extract from these animals with PNGase F, an enzyme that removes N-glycans from N-glycoproteins (Freeze and Kranz, 2010), restored Dpp-GFP migration in mesodermal Pngl knock-down larvae (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: None of the 13 asparagine residues present in GFP conform to the N-glycosylation minimal consensus sequence.
source: None of the 13 asparagine residues present in GFP conform to the N-glycosylation minimal consensus sequence to which the majority of N-glycans are attached (N-X-S/T, where S is serine, T is threonine and X can be any amino acid other than proline) (Taniguchi and Aebi, 2015).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and established knowledge about N-glycosylation consensus sequences.

claim: Pngl deglycosylates a significant fraction of Dpp in Drosophila embryos.
source: These data provide strong evidence that Pngl deglycosylates a significant fraction of Dpp in Drosophila embryos.
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data in Figure 1A showing band shift upon Pngl knockdown.

claim: One copy of dppHA-3NQ partially rescues the lethality of Pngl mutant flies.
source: One copy of dppHA-3NQ partially rescues the lethality of Pngl mutant flies.
evidence: This is supported by eclosion test data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Only 1.3% of dppHA/+ Pngl–/– animals reached adulthood.
source: In agreement with our previous report on Pngl–/– animals (Galeone et al., 2017), only a small fraction (1.3%) of dppHA/+ Pngl–/– animals reached adulthood (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by eclosion test data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Approximately 21% of dppHA-3NQ/+ Pngl–/– animals reached adulthood.
source: However, ~21% of dppHA-3NQ/+ Pngl–/– animals reached adulthood (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by eclosion test data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Loss of BMP signaling in the midgut is only responsible for up to 30% of the lethality in Pngl–/– animals.
source: We have previously reported that loss of BMP signaling in the midgut is only responsible for up to 30% of the lethality in Pngl–/– animals (Galeone et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The BMP-dependent component of Pngl–/– lethality is largely rescued by genetic removal of three N-glycans from Dpp.
source: Therefore, the BMP-dependent component of Pngl–/– lethality is largely rescued by genetic removal of these three N-glycans from Dpp.
evidence: This is inferred from the eclosion test data showing ~21% survival of dppHA-3NQ/+ Pngl–/– animals compared to 1.3% for dppHA/+ Pngl–/– animals.

claim: In control embryos, both dppHA and dppHA-3NQ drive high levels of Dpp expression in PS3 and PS7.
source: In control (Pngl+/–) embryos, both dppHA and dppHA-3NQ drive high levels of Dpp expression in PS3 and PS7 (Figure 1D), similar to endogenous Dpp expression pattern (Galeone et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The pMad expression domain is broader in PS7 of dppHA-3NQ/+ Pngl+/– embryos compared to dppHA/+ Pngl+/– embryos.
source: The pMad expression domain is broader in PS7 of dppHA-3NQ/+ Pngl+/– embryos compared to dppHA/+ Pngl+/– embryos (Figure 1D), suggesting that the 3NQ mutations might enhance BMP signaling in PS7.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The 3NQ mutations might enhance BMP signaling in PS7.
source: The pMad expression domain is broader in PS7 of dppHA-3NQ/+ Pngl+/– embryos compared to dppHA/+ Pngl+/– embryos (Figure 1D), suggesting that the 3NQ mutations might enhance BMP signaling in PS7.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the broader pMad expression domain observed in Figure 1D.

claim: dppHA/+ Pngl–/– embryos show a severe decrease in pMad expression accompanied by weak and narrow Dpp expression domains in PS3 and PS7.
source: Similar to Pngl–/– embryos (Galeone et al., 2017), dppHA/+ Pngl–/– embryos show a severe decrease in pMad expression accompanied by weak and narrow Dpp expression domains in PS3 and PS7 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: One copy of dppHA-3NQ is sufficient to rescue Dpp and pMad expression in PS3 and PS7 of Pngl–/– embryos.
source: Strikingly, one copy of dppHA-3NQ is sufficient to rescue Dpp and pMad expression in PS3 and PS7 of Pngl–/– embryos (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Pngl regulates BMP signaling in the embryonic VM by removing three N-glycans or a subset of them from Dpp.
source: These observations indicate that Pngl regulates BMP signaling in the embryonic VM by removing these three N-glycans or a subset of them from Dpp
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue of BMP signaling by dppHA-3NQ in Pngl–/– embryos.

claim: The N-to-D conversion of N-glycosylated amino acids upon Pngl-mediated deglycosylation is not essential for BMP signaling during Drosophila midgut development.
source: and that the N-to-D conversion of N-glycosylated amino acids upon Pngl-mediated deglycosylation is not essential for BMP signaling during Drosophila midgut development.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that N-to-Q mutations (which do not undergo N-to-D conversion) rescue BMP signaling in Pngl–/– embryos.

claim: Mutating three Dpp N-glycosylation sites does not impair Dpp signaling during embryogenesis.
source: These data indicate that mutating these three Dpp N-glycosylation sites does not impair Dpp signaling during embryogenesis, and suggest that the mutations might even enhance Dpp's range of signaling in the midgut region.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 3NQ mutations might enhance Dpp's range of signaling in the midgut region.
source: These data indicate that mutating these three Dpp N-glycosylation sites does not impair Dpp signaling during embryogenesis, and suggest that the mutations might even enhance Dpp's range of signaling in the midgut region.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the broader pMad expression observed in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: dppHA-3NQ/HA-3NQ animals did not reach adulthood and died by the second instar stage.
source: However, dppHA-3NQ/HA-3NQ animals did not reach adulthood (n = 97) and died by the second instar stage.
evidence: This is based on survival observations of the animals.

claim: The lethality of dppHA-3NQ/HA-3NQ animals is not due to the loss of BMP signaling in the embryos.
source: While we do not know the reason for the lethality of dppHA-3NQ/HA-3NQ animals, the HA and pMad staining data suggest that the lethality is not due to the loss of BMP signaling in the embryos.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that pMad expression is normal or enhanced in dppHA-3NQ/HA-3NQ embryos.

claim: NGLY1 deficiency patients exhibit global developmental delay, seizures, involuntary movements, chronic constipation, osteopenia, small hands and feet, lack of tears and other symptoms.
source: NGLY1 deficiency patients exhibit global developmental delay, seizures, involuntary movements, chronic constipation, osteopenia, small hands and feet, lack of tears and other symptoms (Need et al., 2012; Enns et al., 2014; Lam et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: A loss-of-function mutation in the mouse Ngly1 (Ngly1tm1.1Tasuz) results in late embryonic lethality accompanied by ventricular septal defects.
source: A loss-of-function mutation in the mouse Ngly1 (Ngly1tm1.1Tasuz) results in late embryonic lethality accompanied by ventricular septal defects (VSD) (Fujihira et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: All five Ngly1–/– mutant embryos examined had VSDs.
source: All five Ngly1–/– mutant embryos examined in our studies had VSDs (not shown).
evidence: This is based on examination of mouse embryos.

claim: Ngly1+/+ embryos showed elaborate myocardial trabeculae expressing high level of pSMAD1/5.
source: Ngly1+/+ (control) embryos showed elaborate myocardial trabeculae expressing high level of pSMAD1/5 (Figure 2A, arrowheads).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Ngly1–/– embryos show an overall decrease in the heart size and a remarkable reduction of myocardial trabeculae.
source: We found an overall decrease in the heart size and a remarkable reduction of myocardial trabeculae in mutant embryos (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The remaining trabeculae in Ngly1–/– embryos showed a much weaker pSMAD1/5 staining compared to controls.
source: The remaining trabeculae showed a much weaker pSMAD1/5 staining compared to controls (Figure 2B, arrowhead).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In Ngly1+/+ E15.5 embryos, the choroid plexus consists of slender structures that express high levels of pSMAD1/5 and reach both sides of the ventricle.
source: In Ngly1+/+ E15.5 embryos, the choroid plexus consists of slender structures that express high levels of pSMAD1/5 and reach both sides of the ventricle (Figure 2C and E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and H&E staining data shown in Figures 2C and 2E.

claim: Ngly1–/– embryos have a rudimentary, stump-like choroid plexus with a dramatic decrease in pSMAD1/5 expression.
source: However, Ngly1–/– embryos have a rudimentary, stump-like choroid plexus with a dramatic decrease in pSMAD1/5 expression (Figure 2D and F, arrowheads).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and H&E staining data shown in Figures 2D and 2F.

claim: pSMAD1/5 staining was observed in control E15.5 cerebella but was significantly reduced in mutant cerebella.
source: pSMAD1/5 staining was also observed in control E15.5 cerebella (Figure 2E, arrowheads) but was significantly reduced in mutant cerebella (Figure 2F)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: BMP signaling, mediated by several ligands including BMP4, is essential for normal cardiovascular and choroid plexus development.
source: BMP signaling, mediated by several ligands including BMP4, is essential for normal cardiovascular and choroid plexus development (Hébert et al., 2002; Hébert et al., 2003; Morrell et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: BMP4 is sufficient to induce choroid plexus epithelial fate in neuroepithelial progenitors.
source: and BMP4 is sufficient to induce choroid plexus epithelial fate in neuroepithelial progenitors (Lehtinen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Mouse NGLY1 is required for BMP signaling in specific contexts.
source: Therefore, these data indicate that similar to fly Pngl, mouse NGLY1 is required for BMP signaling in specific contexts
evidence: This is inferred from the decreased pSMAD1/5 expression in Ngly1–/– mouse embryos.

claim: There is a possible causative role between decreased BMP signaling and the observed phenotypes in Ngly1–/– mouse embryos.
source: and suggest a possible causative role between decreased BMP signaling and the observed phenotypes.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the correlation between decreased BMP signaling and developmental abnormalities.

claim: A low level of pSMAD1/5 expression was detected in wild-type MEFs, which did not show a statistically significant decrease in Ngly1–/– MEFs.
source: A low level of pSMAD1/5 expression was detected in wild-type MEFs, which did not show a statistically significant decrease in Ngly1–/– MEFs (Figure 3A,C and D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and western blot data shown in Figures 3A, 3C, and 3D.

claim: Transfection of control MEFs with a construct expressing BMP4HA-Myc resulted in a 12-fold increase in BMP signaling.
source: Transfection of control MEFs with a construct expressing double-tagged BMP4 (HA-tag in the prodomain and Myc-tag in the active domain) resulted in a 12-fold increase in BMP signaling (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and western blot data shown in Figures 3B-D.

claim: BMP signaling in Ngly1–/– MEFs remained at the baseline level upon Bmp4HA-Myc transfection.
source: However, BMP signaling in Ngly1–/– MEFs remained at the baseline level upon Bmp4HA-Myc transfection (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and western blot data shown in Figures 3B-D.

claim: Treating control and Ngly1–/– cells with recombinant BMP4 resulted in similar levels of pSMAD1/5 expression.
source: Of note, treating control and Ngly1–/– cells with recombinant BMP4 resulted in similar levels of pSMAD1/5 expression (Figure 3C,D), indicating that NGLY1 is not essential for receiving the BMP4 signal.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: NGLY1 is not essential for receiving the BMP4 signal.
source: Of note, treating control and Ngly1–/– cells with recombinant BMP4 resulted in similar levels of pSMAD1/5 expression (Figure 3C,D), indicating that NGLY1 is not essential for receiving the BMP4 signal.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Ngly1–/– cells respond normally to exogenous BMP4.

claim: NGLY1 is essential for BMP4 signal-sending in MEFs.
source: Together, these data indicate impaired BMP4 signal-sending in Ngly1–/– MEFs, similar to the impaired Dpp signal-sending observed in Pngl–/– fly VM (Galeone et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Ngly1–/– MEFs fail to induce BMP signaling upon BMP4 transfection but respond normally to exogenous BMP4.

claim: Treating 3T3-L1 cells with low and high concentrations of Z-VAD-fmk resulted in a significant decrease in pSMAD1/5 levels.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, treating 3T3-L1 cells with low and high concentrations of the NGLY1 inhibitor Z-VAD-fluoromethylketone (fmk) (Misaghi et al., 2004) resulted in a significant decrease in pSMAD1/5 levels in these cells, indicating reduced BMP signaling.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 3T3-L1 cells treated with Q-VD-OPh did not exhibit any reduction in the level of pSMAD1/5.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, 3T3-L1 cells treated with Q-VD-OPh did not exhibit any reduction in the level of pSMAD1/5.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: NGLY1 plays a key role in endogenous BMP4 signaling in some contexts.
source: These data are in agreement with our Drosophila and mouse staining results and our MEF overexpression studies, and suggest that NGLY1 plays a key role in endogenous BMP4 signaling in some contexts.
evidence: This is inferred from the Z-VAD-fmk inhibition experiments in 3T3-L1 cells combined with other data in the manuscript.

claim: BMP4HA-Myc only partially localizes to the ER in control MEFs.
source: Double staining for HA and the ER marker KDEL showed that BMP4HA-Myc only partially localizes to the ER in control MEFs (Figure 4A), likely reflecting the exocytic trafficking of BMP4 from ER to Golgi and beyond.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: BMP4HA-Myc almost fully colocalized with KDEL in Ngly1–/– MEFs.
source: In contrast, BMP4HA-Myc almost fully colocalized with KDEL in Ngly1–/– MEFs (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In the absence of NGLY1, BMP4 is trapped in the ER.
source: This suggests that in the absence of NGLY1, BMP4 is trapped in the ER.
evidence: This is inferred from the colocalization of BMP4HA-Myc with the ER marker KDEL in Ngly1–/– MEFs.

claim: The level of GRP78/BiP was significantly increased in control MEFs transfected with Bmp4HA-Myc.
source: As shown in Figure 4B and C, the level of GRP78/BiP was significantly increased in control MEFs transfected with Bmp4HA-Myc, suggesting some BMP4 misfolding in these cells.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: Untransfected Ngly1–/– MEFs showed an increase in GRP78/BiP expression similar to control MEFs transfected with Bmp4HA-Myc.
source: Untransfected Ngly1–/– MEFs also showed a similar increase in GRP78/BiP expression (Figure 4B and C), suggesting some degree of ER stress in these cells (Kozutsumi et al., 1988; Gülow et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: Upon Bmp4HA-Myc transfection, Ngly1–/– cells showed further increase in GRP78/BiP level.
source: Upon Bmp4HA-Myc transfection, Ngly1–/– cells showed further increase in GRP78/BiP level (Figure 4B and C), suggesting that expression of BMP4HA-Myc leads to additional ER stress in Ngly1–/– cells.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: The levels of pIRE1α and OS9 were moderately increased in Ngly1–/– cells.
source: The levels of pIRE1α and OS9 were moderately increased in Ngly1–/– cells, further suggesting that loss of Ngly1 leads to ER stress, potentially due to misfolded glycoprotein accumulation (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: Upon Bmp4HA-Myc transfection, the levels of pIRE1α and OS9 in Ngly1–/– cells increased to 2.5 to 3-fold of pIRE1α and OS9 in untransfected Ngly1–/– cells.
source: Moreover, upon Bmp4HA-Myc transfection, the levels of pIRE1α and OS9 in Ngly1–/– cells increased to 2.5 to 3-fold of pIRE1α and OS9 in untransfected Ngly1–/– cells.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: Bmp4 transfection leads to significant ER stress in Ngly1–/– MEFs, potentially due to the accumulation of misfolded BMP4 in the ER.
source: Together with GRP78 accumulation, these data demonstrate that Bmp4 transfection leads to significant ER stress in Ngly1–/– MEFs, potentially due to the accumulation of misfolded BMP4 in the ER.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased levels of multiple ER stress markers upon BMP4 transfection in Ngly1–/– MEFs.

claim: The cleavages that release the dimerized active domain of BMP ligands from the prodomains are thought to occur in the Golgi apparatus and/or further along the secretory pathway.
source: The full-length BMP proteins dimerize in the ER, but the cleavages that release the dimerized active domain of BMP ligands from the prodomains are thought to occur in the Golgi apparatus and/or further along the secretory pathway (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Nelsen and Christian, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature and illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Conditioned media from Ngly1–/– MEFs showed a severe decrease in the level of BMP4Myc active domain secreted compared to control MEFs.
source: As expected from reduced signaling activity by BMP4HA-Myc in the absence of NGLY1, conditioned media from Ngly1–/– MEFs showed a severe decrease in the level of BMP4Myc active domain secreted by Ngly1–/– cells compared to control MEFs (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Ngly1–/– cells accumulated a band corresponding to the full-length BMP4HA-Myc that migrated slower than the full-length BMP4HA-Myc from control cells in SDS-PAGE gels.
source: Ngly1–/– cells accumulated a band corresponding to the full-length BMP4HA-Myc that migrated slower than the full-length BMP4HA-Myc from control cells in SDS-PAGE gels, compatible with retention of N-glycans upon loss of NGLY1 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Upon digestion with PNGase F and Endo H enzymes, the BMP4HA-Myc band migrated similarly in Ngly1+/+ and Ngly1–/– cells.
source: Upon digestion of the cell lysates with PNGase F and Endo H enzymes (Freeze and Kranz, 2010), the BMP4HA-Myc band migrated similarly in Ngly1+/+ and Ngly1–/– cells, indicating that BMP4 retains ER-type (high mannose) N-glycans in Ngly1–/– cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: BMP4 retains ER-type (high mannose) N-glycans in Ngly1–/– cells.
source: Upon digestion of the cell lysates with PNGase F and Endo H enzymes (Freeze and Kranz, 2010), the BMP4HA-Myc band migrated similarly in Ngly1+/+ and Ngly1–/– cells, indicating that BMP4 retains ER-type (high mannose) N-glycans in Ngly1–/– cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is inferred from the Endo H sensitivity of BMP4HA-Myc in Ngly1–/– cells.

claim: BMP4HA-Myc-4NQ was secreted efficiently by MEFs and was able to induce robust BMP signaling.
source: Moreover, a mutant version of BMP4HA-Myc harboring N-to-Q mutations in all four N-glycosylation sites (BMP4HA-Myc-4NQ) was secreted efficiently by MEFs and was able to induce robust BMP signaling (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: In Ngly1–/– MEFs, BMP4HA-Myc accumulates in the ER and retains ER-type N-glycans.
source: These observations indicate that in Ngly1–/– MEFs, BMP4HA-Myc accumulates in the ER and retains ER-type N-glycans.
evidence: This is inferred from the colocalization with ER markers and Endo H sensitivity data.

claim: Removal of BMP4 N-glycan(s) by NGLY1 is required for BMP4 signaling.
source: The data further support the notion that like Dpp, removal of BMP4 N-glycan(s) by NGLY1 is required for BMP4 signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that BMP4HA-Myc-4NQ signals normally, suggesting that N-glycans themselves are not required but their removal by NGLY1 is.

claim: NGLY1 is likely recruited from the cytosol to the ER membrane via its association with VCP.
source: NGLY1 is likely recruited from the cytosol to the ER membrane via its association with valosin containing protein (VCP; also called p97) (Li et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature and the word 'likely' indicates inference.

claim: VCP is an ATPase which is recruited to the ER upon the accumulation of misfolded proteins in the ER.
source: an ATPase which is recruited to the ER upon the accumulation of misfolded proteins in the ER (Kondratyev et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: VCP plays a critical role in retrotranslocation of misfolded proteins from the ER to cytosol.
source: and plays a critical role in retrotranslocation of misfolded proteins from the ER to cytosol (Ye et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Staining of Ngly1–/– MEFs transfected with NGLY1V5-WT did not show a clear association between NGLY1 and ER without BMP4 transfection.
source: Staining of Ngly1–/– MEFs transfected with an expression vector for a V5-tagged version of wild-type human NGLY1 (NGLY1V5-WT) with anti-V5 and anti-KDEL antibodies did not show a clear association between NGLY1 and ER (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Co-transfection of Bmp4HA-Myc with NGLY1V5-WT resulted in a significant overlap between V5 and KDEL signals.
source: However, co-transfection of Bmp4HA-Myc with NGLY1V5-WT resulted in a significant overlap between V5 and KDEL signals (Figure 5A and B), suggesting that NGLY1 is recruited to the ER upon ER stress, similar to VCP (Kondratyev et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: NGLY1 is recruited to the ER upon ER stress, similar to VCP.
source: However, co-transfection of Bmp4HA-Myc with NGLY1V5-WT resulted in a significant overlap between V5 and KDEL signals (Figure 5A and B), suggesting that NGLY1 is recruited to the ER upon ER stress, similar to VCP (Kondratyev et al., 2007).
evidence: This is inferred from the colocalization of NGLY1 with ER markers upon BMP4 transfection.

claim: ER recruitment of NGLY1 was abolished in both N41P and G79A/F80A mutant versions.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, ER recruitment of NGLY1 was abolished in both mutant versions.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Upon ER stress, NGLY1 is recruited to the ER, potentially through its interaction with VCP.
source: These observations support the notion that upon ER stress, NGLY1 is recruited to the ER, potentially through its interaction with VCP.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that VCP-binding mutants of NGLY1 fail to be recruited to the ER.

claim: Overexpression of NGLY1V5-WT restored BMP4 deglycosylation and signaling in Ngly1–/– MEFs.
source: Overexpression of NGLY1V5-WT restored BMP4 deglycosylation and signaling in Ngly1–/– MEFs (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: NGLY1V5-N41P and NGLY1V5-G79A/F80A failed to promote BMP4 deglycosylation and signaling in Ngly1–/– MEFs despite their comparable expression levels with wild-type NGLY1.
source: However, NGLY1V5-N41P and NGLY1V5-G79A/F80A failed to promote BMP4 deglycosylation and signaling in these cells despite their comparable expression levels with wild-type NGLY1 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: N41, G79 and F80 are conserved between human NGLY1 and fly Pngl.
source: Since N41, G79 and F80 are conserved between human NGLY1 and fly Pngl (Li et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Transgenic expression of human NGLY1WT in the mesoderm fully rescued BMP signaling in Drosophila embryonic midguts.
source: Transgenic expression of human NGLY1WT in the mesoderm fully rescued BMP signaling in Drosophila embryonic midguts (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Transgenic expression of NGLY1N41P and NGLY1G79A/F80A in the mesoderm did not rescue the loss of pMad staining in the VM of Pngl–/– Drosophila embryos.
source: However, transgenic expression of NGLY1N41P and NGLY1G79A/F80A in the mesoderm by Mef2-GAL4 did not rescue the loss of pMad staining in the VM of Pngl–/–Drosophila embryos (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Recombinant NGLY1N41P and NGLY1G79A/F80A show robust enzymatic activity in vitro.
source: Of note, in vitro deglycosylation assays indicated robust enzymatic activity for recombinant NGLY1N41P and NGLY1G79A/F80A (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by enzymatic activity assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Recruitment of NGLY1 molecules from the cytosol to the ER is an evolutionarily conserved step required for BMP4/Dpp deglycosylation and signaling.
source: Together, these data suggest that recruitment of the NGLY1 molecules from the cytosol to the ER is an evolutionarily conserved step required for BMP4/Dpp deglycosylation and signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that VCP-binding mutants fail to rescue BMP signaling in both flies and mammalian cells despite having normal enzymatic activity.

claim: For certain misfolded molecules, blocking proteasomal degradation results in the accumulation of the misfolded protein in the ER.
source: It has previously been reported that for certain misfolded molecules, blocking proteasomal degradation results in the accumulation of the misfolded protein in the ER, suggesting that retrotranslocation and proteasomal degradation are linked for those substrates (Chillarón and Haas, 2000; Saliba et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: BTZ treatment results in the accumulation of a band corresponding in size to deglycosylated BMP4HA-Myc.
source: Anti-HA western blotting showed that BTZ treatment results in the accumulation of a band corresponding in size to deglycosylated BMP4HA-Myc (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figures 6D and 6E.

claim: NGLY1-mediated deglycosylation of BMP4 is normally followed by its proteasomal degradation.
source: This observation suggests that the NGLY1-mediated deglycosylation of BMP4 is normally followed by its proteasomal degradation.
evidence: This is inferred from the accumulation of deglycosylated BMP4 upon proteasome inhibition.

claim: BTZ treatment of wild-type MEFs expressing BMP4HA-Myc did not impair BMP4 signaling.
source: However, BTZ treatment of wild-type MEFs expressing BMP4HA-Myc did not impair BMP4 signaling, as evidenced by pSMAD1/5 expression (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The critical NGLY1-dependent step in BMP4 signaling is the retrotranslocation of misfolded ligands from the ER, not their proteasomal degradation.
source: These observations indicate that the critical NGLY1-dependent step in BMP4 signaling is the retrotranslocation of misfolded ligands from the ER, not their proteasomal degradation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that proteasome inhibition does not impair BMP4 signaling.

claim: The ER lectin OS9 accumulates upon ER stress and forms non-covalent complexes with misfolded glycoproteins to keep them in the ER and transport them to the retrotranslocation machinery.
source: It has been reported that the ER lectin OS9 accumulates upon ER stress and forms non-covalent complexes with misfolded glycoproteins to keep them in the ER and transport them to the retrotranslocation machinery (Bernasconi et al., 2008; Christianson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: BMP4HA-Myc binds endogenous OS9 in Ngly1–/– MEFs.
source: Indeed, co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) experiments indicated that BMP4HA-Myc binds endogenous OS9 (Figure 7A)
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Treating Ngly1–/– MEFs with DTT induced OS9 expression.
source: Treating Ngly1–/– MEFs with DTT also induced OS9 expression (Figure 7A), in agreement with induction of ER protein misfolding by DTT (Lai et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The anti-HA antibody did not IP OS9 in DTT-treated Ngly1–/– MEFs.
source: However, the anti-HA antibody did not IP OS9 in DTT-treated Ngly1–/– MEFs, indicating that the observed IP of OS9 is specifically mediated by BMP4HA-Myc.
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Misfolded BMP4 molecules accumulate in the ER of Ngly1–/– MEFs.
source: These data provide additional evidence that misfolded BMP4 molecules accumulate in the ER of Ngly1–/– MEFs.
evidence: This is inferred from the interaction between BMP4 and OS9, an ER lectin that binds misfolded glycoproteins.

claim: Co-transfection of NGLY1V5-WT with Bmp4HA-Myc into Ngly1–/– MEFs greatly reduced the level of OS9 in these cells.
source: Importantly, co-transfection of NGLY1V5-WT with Bmp4HA-Myc into Ngly1–/– MEFs greatly reduced the level of OS9 in these cells, parallel to a rescue of BMP4 deglycosylation (Figure 7A, OS9 and HA panels).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Co-transfection of NGLY1V5-N41P or NGLY1V5-G79A/F80 failed to reduce OS9 levels and showed a consistent BMP4-OS9 IP.
source: However, co-transfection of NGLY1V5-N41P or NGLY1V5-G79A/F80, which impair the NGLY1-VCP interaction and ER recruitment of NGLY1, failed to reduce OS9 levels and showed a consistent BMP4-OS9 IP.
evidence: This is supported by western blot and co-IP data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Loss of Ngly1 leads to the accumulation of misfolded BMP4 in the ER.
source: These results indicate that loss of Ngly1 leads to the accumulation of misfolded BMP4 in the ER
evidence: This is inferred from the BMP4-OS9 interaction and elevated OS9 levels in Ngly1–/– MEFs.

claim: Interaction of NGLY1 with VCP is critical for retrotranslocation of misfolded BMP4 from the ER into the cytosol.
source: and that interaction of NGLY1 with VCP is critical for retrotranslocation of misfolded BMP4 from the ER into the cytosol.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that VCP-binding mutants of NGLY1 fail to reduce OS9 levels and BMP4-OS9 interaction.

claim: VCP is a critical component of ERAD.
source: VCP is a critical component of ERAD (Ye et al., 2001; Rabinovich et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: NMS-873 treatment led to the accumulation of glycosylated BMP4HA-Myc in MEFs.
source: NMS-873 treatment led to the accumulation of glycosylated BMP4HA-Myc in MEFs (Figure 7B, upper band in HA panel), accompanied by a reduction in the deglycosylated BMP4HA-Myc (Figure 7B, lower band in HA panel) and an increase in the level of GRP78/BiP.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: When the function of VCP is compromised, misfolded BMP4 fails to be deglycosylated by NGLY1 and remains in the ER, thereby inducing ER stress.
source: These observations support the conclusion that when the function of VCP is compromised, misfolded BMP4 fails to be deglycosylated by NGLY1 and remains in the ER, thereby inducing ER stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the accumulation of glycosylated BMP4 and increased GRP78/BiP upon VCP inhibition.

claim: Combination of NMS-873 and BTZ resulted in the accumulation of deglycosylated BMP4HA-Myc and an enhanced accumulation of glycosylated BMP4HA-Myc and GRP78/BiP compared to cells treated with NMS-873 alone.
source: Combination of NMS-873 and BTZ resulted in the accumulation of deglycosylated BMP4HA-Myc and an enhanced accumulation of glycosylated BMP4HA-Myc and GRP78/BiP compared to cells treated with NMS-873 alone.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: BMP4 is an ERAD substrate.
source: Together, these data provide compelling evidence that BMP4 is an ERAD substrate.
evidence: This is inferred from the VCP inhibition experiments and other data showing BMP4 accumulation in the ER and interaction with ERAD components.

claim: SKN-1/NFE2L1 has recently been shown to be a direct target of N-glycanase one in worms and mammalian cells.
source: An unusual ER membrane protein whose ER luminal domain contains DNA-binding and transactivation domains (SKN-1 in C. elegans, NFE2L1 or NRF1 in mammals) has recently been shown to be a direct target of N-glycanase one in worms and mammalian cells (Tomlin et al., 2017; Lehrbach et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: In cells with normal proteasome function, NFE2L1 is retrotranslocated from the ER in a VCP-dependent manner and undergoes proteasomal degradation.
source: In cells with normal proteasome function, NFE2L1 is retrotranslocated from the ER in a VCP-dependent manner and undergoes proteasomal degradation (Steffen et al., 2010; Radhakrishnan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Upon impaired proteasomal function, SKN-1/NFE2L1 undergoes deglycosylation and N-to-D sequence editing by PNG-1/NGLY1 and cleavage by a conserved cytoplasmic protease, and enters the nucleus to activate the transcription of proteasomal components.
source: However, upon impaired proteasomal function, SKN-1/NFE2L1 undergoes deglycosylation and N-to-D sequence editing by PNG-1/NGLY1 and cleavage by a conserved cytoplasmic protease, and enters the nucleus to activate the transcription of proteasomal components, a process known as proteasome bounce-back response (Radhakrishnan et al., 2010; Lehrbach and Ruvkun, 2016; Tomlin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Treatment of Ngly1+/+ MEFs with BTZ induced the expression of proteasomal genes Psmb1, Psmb4 and Psmb7.
source: In agreement with a previous report (Tomlin et al., 2017), treatment of Ngly1+/+ MEFs with BTZ induced the expression of proteasomal genes Psmb1, Psmb4 and Psmb7 (Figure 8A–C)
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 8A-C.

claim: In Ngly1–/– cells, the proteasome bounce-back response was completely lost.
source: but in Ngly1–/– cells this response was completely lost (Figure 8A–C, arrows).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 8A-C.

claim: Overexpression of human NGLY1V5-WT rescued the proteasome bounce-back phenotype in Ngly1–/– MEFs.
source: Overexpression of human NGLY1V5-WT rescued this phenotype in Ngly1–/– MEFs (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 8A-C.

claim: The proteasomal bounce-back was restored by NGLY1V5-N41P and NGLY1V5-G79A/F80A in Ngly1–/– MEFs.
source: Notably, unlike BMP4 signaling, the proteasomal bounce-back was also restored by NGLY1V5-N41P and NGLY1V5-G79A/F80A in Ngly1–/– MEFs (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 8A-C.

claim: The deglycosylation/N-to-D editing of NFE2L1 N-glycosylation sites does not depend on NGLY1's ER recruitment and can be mediated by the cytosolic pool of NGLY1.
source: These observations indicate that the deglycosylation/N-to-D editing of NFE2L1 N-glycosylation sites does not depend on NGLY1's ER recruitment and can be mediated by the cytosolic pool of NGLY1.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that VCP-binding mutants of NGLY1 can still rescue the proteasome bounce-back response.

claim: Upon accumulation of misfolded BMP4 in the ER, some NGLY1 molecules are recruited to the ER.
source: Specifically, we propose that upon accumulation of misfolded BMP4 in the ER, some NGLY1 molecules are recruited to the ER
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The VCP-mediated retrotranslocation of misfolded BMP4 molecules can only be efficiently completed upon deglycosylation by NGLY1 molecules recruited to the cytosolic surface of the ER.
source: and that the VCP-mediated retrotranslocation of misfolded BMP4 molecules can only be efficiently completed upon deglycosylation by NGLY1 molecules recruited to the cytosolic surface of the ER (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: Mutations that abolish NGLY1's VCP binding impair its ER recruitment and prevent NGLY1 from deglycosylating BMP4.
source: (3) Mutations that abolish NGLY1's VCP binding impair its ER recruitment and prevent NGLY1 from deglycosylating BMP4, rescuing BMP4 signaling in Ngly1–/– MEFs, and rescuing Dpp signaling in Pngl–/– embryos (Figures 5 and 6)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of VCP in Ngly1+/+ cells results in the accumulation of a glycosylated form of BMP4HA-Myc and induction of ER stress.
source: and (4) Pharmacological inhibition of VCP in Ngly1+/+ cells results in the accumulation of a glycosylated form of BMP4HA-Myc and induction of ER stress (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Blocking the function of proteasome does not impair the ability of control MEFs to send the BMP4 signal.
source: We note that blocking the function of proteasome does not impair the ability of control MEFs to send the BMP4 signal, even though a deglycosylated form of BMP4 accumulates in these cells.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The critical NGLY1-dependent step in BMP4 signaling is retrotranslocation of misfolded BMP4 molecules from the ER.
source: This suggests that even though NGLY1 ultimately promotes the proteasomal degradation of misfolded BMP4 molecules, the critical NGLY1-dependent step in BMP4 signaling is retrotranslocation of misfolded BMP4 molecules from the ER.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that proteasome inhibition does not impair BMP4 signaling.

claim: Mutations affecting the cleavage or folding of some BMP and TGFβ family ligands can block the secretion and activity of wild-type BMP and/or TGFβ ligands in a dominant-negative fashion.
source: Previous studies have reported that mutations affecting the cleavage or folding of some BMP and TGFβ family ligands can block the secretion and activity of wild-type BMP and/or TGFβ ligands in a dominant-negative fashion, likely through generation of non-productive dimers with wild-type ligands (Lopez et al., 1992; Hawley et al., 1995; Suzuki et al., 1997b; Thomas et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: NGLY1 helps clear the misfolded BMP4 precursor monomers from the ER, thereby reducing the possibility that nonfunctional dimers consisting of misfolded and properly folded BMP4 will form.
source: Accordingly, a likely scenario for the role of NGLY1 in BMP4 signaling is that it helps clear the misfolded BMP4 precursor monomers from the ER, thereby reducing the possibility that nonfunctional dimers consisting of misfolded and properly folded BMP4 will form.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the data and established knowledge about BMP ligand biology.

claim: Clearing misfolded BMP4 precursor monomers from the ER promotes the formation of properly folded BMP4 precursor dimers that can be transported out of the ER to be cleaved to generate the functional ligand.
source: This, in turn, promotes the formation of properly folded BMP4 precursor dimers that can be transported out of the ER to be cleaved to generate the functional ligand.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the data and established knowledge about BMP ligand biology.

claim: When N-glycosylation sites of Dpp are ablated by NQ mutations, it no longer depends on Pngl for signaling in the fly midgut.
source: Notably, when N-glycosylation sites of Dpp are ablated by NQ mutations, it no longer depends on Pngl for signaling in the fly midgut (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The critical role played by NGLY1 in BMP signaling is direct removal of N-glycans from misfolded Dpp/BMP4.
source: These observations strongly suggest that the critical role played by NGLY1 in this context is direct removal of N-glycans from misfolded Dpp/BMP4.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue of BMP signaling by N-glycosylation site mutations.

claim: The misfolded versions of Dpp3NQ and BMP4HA-Myc-4NQ can be efficiently retrotranslocated independently of Pngl/NGLY1, potentially by a glycosylation-independent ERAD pathway.
source: Considering the above-mentioned model, our data suggest that the misfolded versions of Dpp3NQ and BMP4HA-Myc-4NQ can be efficiently retrotranslocated independently of Pngl/NGLY1, potentially by a previously reported, glycosylation-independent ERAD pathway, which heavily depends on GRP78/BiP (Ushioda et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the data and established knowledge about ERAD pathways.

claim: NFE2L1 has been identified as an evolutionarily-conserved, direct target of NGLY1.
source: Recent studies have identified NFE2L1 as an evolutionarily-conserved, direct target of NGLY1 (Lehrbach and Ruvkun, 2016; Tomlin et al., 2017; Lehrbach et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Deglycosylation of NFE2L1 by NGLY1 leads to its activation.
source: First, deglycosylation of NFE2L1 by NGLY1 leads to its activation.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about NFE2L1 function.

claim: Deglycosylation of BMP4 by NGLY1 promotes its proteasomal degradation.
source: However, deglycosylation of BMP4 by NGLY1 promotes its proteasomal degradation.
evidence: This is supported by data showing accumulation of deglycosylated BMP4 upon proteasome inhibition.

claim: The cytoplasmic pool of NGLY1 is capable of deglycosylating NFE2L1.
source: Second, the cytoplasmic pool of NGLY1 is capable of deglycosylating NFE2L1, suggesting that NFE2L1 retrotranslocation does not depend on NGLY1.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that VCP-binding mutants of NGLY1 can rescue the proteasome bounce-back response.

claim: NFE2L1 retrotranslocation does not depend on NGLY1.
source: Second, the cytoplasmic pool of NGLY1 is capable of deglycosylating NFE2L1, suggesting that NFE2L1 retrotranslocation does not depend on NGLY1.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that VCP-binding mutants of NGLY1 can rescue the proteasome bounce-back response.

claim: Only the ER-recruited pool of NGLY1 seems to be able to deglycosylate BMP4.
source: However, only the ER-recruited pool of NGLY1 seems to be able to deglycosylate BMP4, suggesting a role in BMP4 retrotranslocation.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that VCP-binding mutants of NGLY1 fail to rescue BMP4 signaling.

claim: NGLY1 plays a role in BMP4 retrotranslocation.
source: However, only the ER-recruited pool of NGLY1 seems to be able to deglycosylate BMP4, suggesting a role in BMP4 retrotranslocation.
evidence: This is inferred from the requirement for ER-recruited NGLY1 for BMP4 deglycosylation.

claim: The key role of PNG-1/NGLY1 on SKN-1/NFE2L1 in C. elegans is not the removal of the N-glycans per se, but is the N-to-D sequence editing of NFE2L1 N-glycosylation sites.
source: Third, the key role of PNG-1/NGLY1 on SKN-1/NFE2L1 in C. elegans is not the removal of the N-glycans per se, but is the N-to-D sequence editing of NFE2L1 N-glycosylation sites (Lehrbach et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Pngl/NGLY1 regulates BMP signaling by removing N-glycans from misfolded Dpp/BMP4, and N-to-D editing is not essential for the function of Dpp/BMP4.
source: However, our data suggest that Pngl/NGLY1 regulates BMP signaling by removing N-glycans from misfolded Dpp/BMP4, and that N-to-D editing is not essential for the function of Dpp/BMP4.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that N-to-Q mutations rescue BMP signaling in Pngl–/– embryos.

claim: NGLY1 deficiency affects multiple organ systems in human patients.
source: NGLY1 deficiency affects multiple organ systems in human patients (Need et al., 2012; Enns et al., 2014; Lam et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: The molecular basis for the developmental phenotypes of NGLY1 deficiency has remained elusive.
source: However, despite the recent advances in understanding the function of NGLY1 and its homologs, the molecular basis for the developmental phenotypes of this disease has remained elusive.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge.

claim: pSMAD1/5 staining in E15.5 Ngly1–/– mouse embryos shows impaired BMP signaling in certain tissues, including the 4th ventricle choroid plexus.
source: In agreement with the tissue-specific defects observed in Pngl-mutant flies (Galeone et al., 2017), pSMAD1/5 staining in E15.5 Ngly1–/– mouse embryos shows impaired BMP signaling in certain tissues, including the 4th ventricle choroid plexus.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Some of the NGLY1 deficiency patient phenotypes (including neurological deficits and orthopedic features) may be caused by altered BMP signaling.
source: Future work will clarify whether any of the patient phenotypes (including neurological deficits and orthopedic features [Cahan and Frick, 2019]) are caused by altered BMP signaling.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.
